extracted.intended_audience: filmmakers, comedy writers, TV/film students and fans interested in humorous credit design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for creating or evaluating humorous opening/closing credits in films and television, showing techniques that subvert, extend, or play with conventional credit sequences for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits-as-diegetic-prop
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate title/credits into the scene so the onscreen text is treated as a physical element in the world (title appears on a marquee, poster, or over a character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom — film title appears during a musical number so Willie appears to be standing in front of the words; Ocean's 11 (original) — Rat Pack walk past a marquee with their names. Use when the visual gag gains from characters interacting with credit text; avoid when it obscures readability or distracts from performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits-as-running-gag-continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend a running gag into the credits (credits themselves carry the joke or continue a recurring joke from the work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Deadpool's opening credits filled with jokes and descriptive labels; State and Main's gag about promised 'associate producer' credits; Monty Python prolonging running gags into end credits. Use when credits are a natural place to keep the joke going; ensure the gag doesn't undercut necessary acknowledgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional_or_in-universe_credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit fictional in-universe entities, companies, characters, or sponsors as if they were real contributors to the production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Running Man's announcer credits fictional sponsors; Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy's Karla Films; The Man from U.N.C.L.E.'s 'acknowledgment' to a fictitious organization. Good for world-building and satire; clarity matters if viewers might mistake fiction for real credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous_role_descriptions_and_labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace standard job/role names with comedic or descriptive labels (e.g., 'God's perfect idiot', 'A gratuitous cameo', 'An entirely CGI character').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Deadpool's cast descriptions; Deadpool's crew jokes ('Produced by Asshats'); credits listing 'Finding Uterus' or 'Fly Handler' in Ten 2014. Use to lampoon industry conventions or characters; avoid insulting actual contributors unless consensual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake_or_anachronistic_disclaimers_and_legalese
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parody disclaimers, copyright notices, or legal warnings as jokes (mock warnings, legal-sounding statements that are comedic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Richard Donner's anti-fur disclaimer added to Superman II Re-Cut; RoboCop's 'criminal prosecution by enforcement droids'; multiple 'No X were harmed' disclaimers (Guardians of the Galaxy, Harry Potter's 'No dragons were harmed'). Effective for satirical commentary or tonal contrast; be cautious with genuine legal content or causing real-world misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit-order_manipulation_for_comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the normal ordering of credits (alphabetical, prominence, order of appearance) for humorous effect: order by height, cowardice, disappearance, or other invented schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Bed Sitting Room billed stars in order of height; Up Pompeii! lists cast by order of disappearance; Up the Front lists by 'order of cowardice'. Useful to create a reveal or punchline during credits; ensure viewers can still identify principal cast when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-credit_or_post-credit_stinger_setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Use credits to set up or conceal a stinger/teaser (credit a character before they appear or use credits to transition to a post-credits scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Resident Evil: Afterlife credits Jill Valentine before her stinger appearance; MCU films credit 'hero will return' as an in-credit tease; credits that cut to an extra scene a few seconds after a name appears. Effective for surprise or to reward viewers who stay; timing and pacing are important so stinger impact isn't spoiled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic_and_graphic_thematic_variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alter typography, script, colors, or visual language of credits to reflect the film's world or themes (foreign scripts, tribe colors, runes, mirrored credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Black Panther displays credits in Wakandan script and tribe-specific colors; The Northman uses ancient Norse runes; Remastered 'Backwards' runs credits as mirror image. Helps reinforce setting/immersion or produce a visual joke; maintain legibility or provide translation when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits_as_character_or_cast_joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit characters or nontraditional 'performers' (animals, monsters, objects) as if they were actors, or credit roles that didn't appear to create surprise or humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Godzilla: King of the Monsters lists monsters 'as themselves'; Dora and the Lost City of Gold includes Fiesta Trio curtain call; Harry Potter dragon disclaimer. Can be affectionate, meta, or an in-joke for fans; be transparent when union/contractual rules require real credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden_easter_eggs_in_credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hide codes, recipes, jokes, anagrams, or extra content in the credits (cheat codes, anagrammed names, recipe listings, thank-you lists with jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mortal Kombat: The Movie hides an MK3 cheat code; S1m0ne replaces I/O with 1/0 and has programmer in thank-you list; Ten 2014's 'Finding Uterus' in-joke. Great for attentive viewers and DVD/streaming bonus content; avoid essential plot information that viewers who skip credits would miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical_and_thematic_credit_variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alter the music or arrangement during credit sequences to match episode theme, tone, or parody (new arrangement, lyrics, or performed by characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: How I Met Your Mother cast perform theme; Buffy 'Once More With Feeling' features altered credits; various TV episodes re-score credits in period/genre styles. Use to extend the episode's style; ensure licensing and performer permissions for alternate arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-crediting_and_authorial_jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit authors, creators, or production roles with meta or self-referential phrasing (pseudonyms, fictional co-authors, authorial asides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Adaptation. credits 'Charlie and Donald Kaufman' (one fictional); Terry Pratchett credited as 'mucking about with the script' in Hogfather; Thursday Next novels include filmlike credits and 'warnings' in book copyright pages. Effective for literary/meta humor; be careful with contractual name requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits_breaking_or_subverting_broadcast_conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use credits to subvert expectations about how credits are presented on broadcast (rolling at odd times, pauses, reversing, airing credits early to annoy DVRs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Breaking Bad delays credits in 'Ozymandias' and pauses to time an emotional beat; Have I Got News for You started credits at the beginning to annoy recorders; Monty Python and others ran credits immediately after opening titles. Useful for surprising or commenting on medium conventions; consider broadcaster rules and viewer accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful_crediting_of_nonhumans_or_objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit nonhuman participants, props, background items or even foods/objects in 'Special Thanks' or cast/crew lists as a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Special Thanks' to 'Steak (the Food)' in The Recovered; credits listing a dead housefly as 'Mervin Fly' and 'Fly Handler'; Psalty's credits include a cookie recipe. Works as low-stakes silliness; avoid confusing audiences when real contributions must be acknowledged.
